part_title: Cloud Service Models, Responsibility and Pricing
review_basis: Original AIF M02 slides 14–17 personally reviewed, including IaaS/PaaS/SaaS diagrams, service management matrix, house analogy and compute-storage-transfer cost drivers.

scenes.title: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
scenes.narration: This slide introduces three ways people buy and use cloud services. Read it from left to right, starting with Infrastructure as a Service, or IaaS. Infrastructure means the fundamental computing building blocks: virtual servers, storage and networking. A virtual server is a computer created in software that runs on a cloud provider's physical infrastructure. With IaaS you get considerable flexibility, but you still configure and protect the operating system, applications and data. Amazon EC2 is an AWS example. Next is Platform as a Service, or PaaS. Here the provider manages more of the environment needed to deploy an application. Instead of installing and maintaining every server component, a development team concentrates on its application code and data. Imagine a graduate building a college event registration app. They might prefer a managed application platform to avoid spending all their time on server maintenance. On the right is Software as a Service, or SaaS. This is a complete application ready to use, often through a browser. A hosted email or collaboration product is an example. You do not write the email application's code or run its servers, although you still choose account permissions and handle your information appropriately. The bottom takeaway says choose the highest-level service that meets your needs. Higher-level does not mean universally better: sometimes you need special operating system settings and more control, in which case IaaS may fit. Quick check: a team wants to develop its own app without managing underlying servers. Which model fits the general requirement? PaaS. A student wants to send email through a ready-made product. That is SaaS. Distinguish what you want to build from what you simply want to use.

scenes.title: Who manages each layer?
scenes.narration: This chart makes cloud responsibility concrete. Across the top are four approaches: on premises, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Down the left are layers: applications, data, runtime, middleware, operating system, virtualization, servers, storage and networking. Runtime means the software environment that executes an application; middleware is supporting software that connects different components. In the first column, on premises, the customer operates the entire stack. In IaaS, shown with Amazon EC2, AWS handles the underlying physical infrastructure and virtualization while the customer usually manages the guest operating system, installed software, applications and data. In the PaaS example, Elastic Beanstalk manages additional platform tasks, though customers remain responsible for application code, data and important configuration decisions. In SaaS, the provider manages the ready-made application and underlying systems. The purple and cyan checks are simplified ownership indicators, not a substitute for each service's official shared responsibility documentation. For example, in a hosted email service, the provider maintains the software, but the customer still controls who gets an account, what sensitive information is stored, and which staff may read it. The shield on the right emphasizes that increased management by AWS never eliminates customer security responsibilities. An organization may still have to manage identity, data classification, governance and permissible use. Think of renting a furnished apartment. The landlord may maintain the building, but you must lock your door and look after your belongings. The responsibility varies by contract, and cloud services vary similarly. Practice question: if an EC2 server runs outdated application software, does AWS automatically patch every application inside it? Generally no; the customer must manage its guest software. Always confirm the actual service boundary.

scenes.title: Choosing between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
scenes.narration: We can now make a cloud decision from requirements rather than memorizing acronyms. The left column shows IaaS as layers of infrastructure, operating system and application. The provider supplies the physical foundation, but the customer manages more of the operating environment. The center shows PaaS: the provider also manages much of the runtime, middleware and operating system, leaving the team to focus mainly on its code and data. On the right, SaaS supplies a ready-to-use application. The wording 'provider manages everything' in the illustration describes much of the technical stack, not the customer's identity or information security obligations. For an easy analogy, look at the three houses at the bottom. IaaS is like receiving a foundation and building the house to your preferences. PaaS is a structure already prepared for you to finish. SaaS is a furnished house you can move into and use. The analogy isn't exact, but it illustrates control versus convenience. An organization that needs to install specialized operating system software could favor a virtual machine such as Amazon EC2. A developer team that mainly wants to upload its application may prefer a managed platform. Employees who need a completed document-sharing service could simply use SaaS. Notice the examples name Elastic Beanstalk as a platform service and other vendors' managed platforms; the principles are not exclusive to AWS. Some managed AI services also hide substantial infrastructure complexity, but not every AI API maps neatly into the SaaS category. Finally, choose the service with the right combination of operational responsibility, control, cost and security. Quick check: would using SaaS mean the team never needs account permissions or data protection policies? No, those customer responsibilities remain.

scenes.title: Cloud pricing: understand the cost drivers
scenes.narration: Cloud pricing becomes easier when we separate the major things that are measured. Trace the picture from the user request to compute, storage and then network transfer. Compute is the processing work performed by servers or managed services. A virtual machine may have a cost based on its size and running duration, while an AI inference service might charge according to input and output tokens or request units. A token is a small piece of text processed by a language model, not exactly the same as a word. The center storage cylinder holds files, datasets and perhaps model outputs. Storage may be charged by the amount stored, how long it remains there, and sometimes requests or retrieval. Finally look at the two arrows around the cloud. Data coming into a provider is often not charged as internet data transfer, while data leaving the provider may incur charges depending on the service, destination and route. This varies, and region-to-region or other internal transfers can have their own charges. The slide therefore says to check current pricing rather than memorize one fixed rate. Imagine students running a weekend AI project. A computer running continuously for the entire weekend may cost more than one used for an hour. A stored dataset continues consuming storage after the experiment ends. And sending large outputs to thousands of users may add network costs. Pay as you go means consumption affects your bill; it does not mean every product is free when nobody is actively typing into it. A useful habit is to estimate cost before using a service, monitor actual charges, and delete unneeded resources. Quick question: an unused but running virtual server, a forgotten storage volume, and outbound data traffic can all contribute to the bill. Which is the safest answer? All three. Cost management is an architectural responsibility, not just an accounting task.
